cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XI
The dead: Tiresias' prophecy, Anticleia, the heroines, Agamemnon, Achilles, Ajax.
And when we had come down to the ship and the sea,
first of all we hauled the ship\ndown to the bright salt water,
and set the mast and the sails in the black ship,\nand took the sheep and put them aboard, and ourselves
went aboard grieving, letting the big tears fall.
And for us, behind the dark-blue-prowed ship,\na following wind that filled the sail, a good companion,
was sent by Circe of the lovely braids,\ndread goddess with a mortal's voice.
So when we had seen to the tackle through the ship,
we sat, and the wind and the steersman held her on course.
All day long her sail was\nstretched as she crossed the water;
and the sun went down, and all the ways grew dark.
She came to the limits of deep-flowing Ocean.
There is the land and city of the Cimmerian men,\nshrouded in mist and cloud: never does the shining
sun look down on them with his rays,\nnot when he climbs toward the starry heaven,
when he turns back from heaven to earth,\nbut deadly night is stretched over wretched mortals.
Coming there we beached the ship, and took out\nthe sheep, and walked along the stream of Ocean
until we came to the place that Circe had appointed.
There Perimedes and Eurylochus held the victims,\nand I drew the sharp sword from beside my thigh
and dug a pit about a cubit's measure this way and that,
and around it I poured a drink-offering to all the dead —
first with milk and honey mingled, then with sweet wine,
the third time with water;\nand I sprinkled white barley over it.
And I entreated, over and over,\nthe strengthless heads of the dead:
vowing that, come to Ithaca, I would offer in my halls
a barren heifer, my best,\nand heap the pyre with good things;
and to Tiresias, apart, alone, I would sacrifice a ram
all black, the one that stands out from all our flocks.
And when with vows and prayers I had entreated them,
the tribes of the dead,\nI took the sheep and cut their throats
over the pit, and the dark-clouded\nblood ran; and they gathered,
the souls of the dead who are gone, up out of Erebus:
brides, and unwed youths,\nand old men worn by long suffering,
and tender girls with the fresh grief on their hearts,\nand many men gashed by the bronze-tipped spears,
men killed in war, in armor caked with their blood.
In crowds from every side they came flocking about the pit
with a sound that had no earthly likeness;\nand the pale terror took me.
Then I roused my companions, and commanded them
to flay the sheep that lay there slaughtered by the\npitiless bronze, and burn them, and pray to the gods —
to mighty Hades and dread Persephone; and I myself,\ndrawing the sharp sword from beside my thigh,
sat there, and would not let the\nstrengthless heads of the dead
come near the blood before I had questioned Tiresias.
First came the soul of my companion Elpenor,\nfor he was not yet buried under the wide-wayed earth:
we had left his body behind in Circe's hall,\nunwept and unburied, since another task was driving us.
I wept to see him, and my heart pitied him,\nand lifting my voice I spoke winged words to him:
'Elpenor — how did you come here, under the misty dark?
You have outstripped me —\non foot, and I in my black ship.'
So I spoke, and he groaned aloud, and answered:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices,
the evil doom of a god blinded me —\nthat, and wine past measure.
Lying down to sleep in Circe's hall, I never\nthought to come back down again by the long ladder;
I fell headlong from the roof, and my neck snapped\nfrom the spine; and my soul came down to Hades.
Now I beg you — by those left behind,\nthose not here beside us:
by your wife; by your father,\nwho reared you when you were small;
by Telemachus, whom you left an only child in your halls.
For I know that when you go from here,\nfrom the house of Hades,
you will put in again with your\nwell-made ship at the island of Aeaea:
there, my lord, I charge you: remember me.
Do not go on and leave me behind you unwept, unburied,
turning away — lest I become a\ncause of gods' wrath against you —
but burn me with all the armor that is mine,\nand heap me a mound on the shore of the gray salt sea:
an unlucky man's marker, for men to come to learn of.
Accomplish this for me — and fix upon the mound the oar
I rowed with when I lived,\nwhen I was among my companions.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'All this, poor luckless man, I will accomplish and do.'
So the two of us sat trading grim words,\nI on one side, holding my sword over the blood,
and across from me the phantom\nof my companion, talking on.
Then came the soul of my dead mother,\nAnticleia, daughter of great-hearted Autolycus,
whom I had left alive when I went to holy Ilium.
I wept to see her, and my heart pitied her;\nbut even so, for all my thick grief, I would not let her
come near the blood before I had questioned Tiresias.
Then came the soul of Theban Tiresias,\nholding a golden scepter; and he knew me, and spoke:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —
what now, unlucky man?\nWhy have you left the light of the sun
and come to see the dead, and this place without joy?
Draw back from the pit; hold off your sharp sword,
so that I may drink of the blood,\nand tell you the unerring truth.'
So he spoke, and I stepped back,\nand drove the silver-studded sword
home in its sheath. And when he had drunk the dark blood,\nthen at last the blameless seer addressed me:
'It is honey-sweet homecoming you seek, shining Odysseus,
and a god will make it grim for you. For I do not think
the shaker of earth will fail to see you —\nthe grudge is set in his heart,
raging because you blinded his dear son.
Yet even so, though you suffer evils,\nyou may still come home,
if you are willing to hold hard\nyour own heart and your companions',
from the hour when you first bring your well-made ship\nin to the island Thrinacia, escaping the violet sea,
and find at pasture there the cattle and the strong flocks
of Helios, who sees all things and hears all things.
If you leave them unharmed,\nand keep your mind on homecoming,
then you may yet reach Ithaca, though you suffer evils.
But if you harm them, then I foretell destruction for\nship and companions; and even if you yourself escape,
late you will come, and in evil case, all companions lost,
on another man's ship; and you will find trouble in\nyour house — overweening men, who eat away your living,
courting your godlike wife and offering bride-gifts.
Yet, truly, you will come and repay their violence.
And when you have killed the suitors in your halls,\nwhether by guile or in the open, with the sharp bronze,
then go on a journey, taking a well-shaped oar,\nuntil you come to men who know nothing of the sea,
men who eat no food that is mixed with salt,\nwho know nothing of red-cheeked ships,
nothing of well-shaped oars, which are wings for ships.
And I will tell you a sign,\nunmistakable: it will not escape you.
When another traveler, meeting you on the road,\nsays you carry a winnowing-fan on your shining shoulder,
then and there fix the well-shaped oar in the\nearth and offer fine victims to the lord Poseidon —
a ram, a bull, and a boar that has mounted sows —\nand turn away home, and offer holy hecatombs
to the deathless gods who hold wide heaven,\nto all of them, each in order. And death will come to you
from the sea, so gentle a death, and take you worn\ndown under sleek old age; and around you the peoples
will be prosperous. This I tell you is unerring truth.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Tiresias — all that, no doubt,\nthe gods themselves have spun.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly.
I see here the soul of my dead mother:
she sits in silence near the blood,\nand cannot bring herself
to look her own son in the face.
Tell me, lord: how may she know me for the man I am?'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'An easy word I will tell you, and set it in your mind.
Whomever of the dead who are gone you allow to\ncome near the blood, that one will speak you truth;
whomever you begrudge it, that one will draw back and go.'
So speaking, the soul of the lord Tiresias went back
into the house of Hades, when he\nhad told out the decrees of fate.
But I stayed rooted where I was until my mother
came and drank the dark-clouded blood. And at once\nshe knew me, and wailing she spoke winged words to me:
'My child — how did you come here, under the misty dark,
alive? Hard it is for the living to look on all this:
for between lie great rivers, and terrible waters —\nOcean first of all, which there is no crossing on foot,
never, unless a man has a well-made ship.
Are you only now come wandering here from Troy —
after all this time — with ship\nand companions? Have you not yet
been to Ithaca — not seen your wife in your own halls?'
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
'Mother, need brought me down to Hades:
to consult the soul of Theban Tiresias.
For not yet have I come near Achaea — not yet
set foot on our own land;\nI have wandered without pause, in misery,
since the day I first followed noble Agamemnon toward\nIlium of the fine horses, to fight the Trojans.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
what doom of death, that lays men low, mastered you?
A long illness? Or did Artemis the arrow-pourer\ncome with her gentle arrows, and kill you?
And tell me of my father, and the son I left behind:
does my honor still rest safe\nwith them, or does some other
man hold it now — do they say I will come home no more?
And tell me the mind and purpose of my wedded wife:
does she stay by the boy and keep all things safe?
Or has the best man of the Achaeans married her already?'
So I spoke, and at once my honored mother answered:
'Oh yes — she stays, and more: with an enduring heart\nshe is there in your halls; and always in misery
her nights waste away, and her days, in tears.
Your fine honor no man holds yet: at his ease\nTelemachus farms the estates unchallenged, and feasts
at the equal banquets it is fitting\na lawgiving man should tend:
for all men issue him the summons.\nBut your father stays out there
on the farm, and never comes down to the city. Bedding
he has none — no bedstead, no cloaks, no shining blankets:
through the winter he sleeps\nwhere the slaves do, in the house,
in the ashes by the fire, and puts poor clothing on\nhis skin; but when summer comes, and the heavy autumn,
then anywhere along the rise of his vineyard plot a\nbed of fallen leaves is thrown on the ground for him,
and there he lies grieving,\nand the sorrow grows great in his heart,
aching for your homecoming; and hard old age comes on him.
And so it was with me: so I too died and met my doom.
Not in the halls did the keen-eyed arrow-pourer\ncome with her gentle arrows and kill me;
no illness fell upon me, of the kind that most often\ndraws the life from the limbs in hateful wasting:
no — it was longing for you,\nyour counsels, shining Odysseus,
your gentle-heartedness,\nthat robbed me of honey-sweet life.'
So she spoke; and I, my mind stirred,\nlonged to take the soul of my dead mother in my arms.
Three times I started toward her,\nand my heart bade me hold her;
three times, out of my hands, like a shadow or a dream
she flew. And the grief grew\nsharper in my heart each time,
and lifting my voice I spoke winged words to her:
'Mother — why will you not stay\nfor me, when I long to hold you,
so that even here in Hades,\nthrowing our arms around each other,
the two of us might take our fill of icy mourning?
Or is this a phantom queenly Persephone has sent me,\nso that I may weep and groan the more?'
So I spoke, and at once my honored mother answered:
'Ah me, my child, luckless beyond all mortal men —
in no way does Persephone,\nthe daughter of Zeus, deceive you:
this is the settled way of mortals, when one dies.
The sinews no longer hold the flesh and bones together:
all that, the strong fury of the blazing fire breaks down,\nas soon as the life has left the white bones,
and the soul flits away like a dream, and hovers.
But press on toward the light,\nas fast as you can. And mark
all these things — to tell them to your wife hereafter.'
So the two of us traded words. And then the women\ncame — for queenly Persephone sent them on —
all who had been the wives and daughters of the great.
They came flocking in crowds around the dark blood,\nand I considered how I might question each in turn.
And this, as I turned it over, seemed to me the best plan:
drawing the long-edged sword from beside my thick thigh,
I would not let them drink the dark blood all together.
So they came up one by one, in file, and each\ndeclared her lineage; and I questioned them all.
There the first I saw was Tyro, born of a noble father,\nwho said she was the child of blameless Salmoneus,
and called herself the wife of Cretheus, Aeolus' son.
She fell in love with a river — divine Enipeus,\nfar the most beautiful of rivers flowing on the earth —
and she would haunt Enipeus' beautiful streams.
And the earth-holder, the shaker\nof earth, took the river's likeness
and lay beside her at the mouths of the eddying water;
and a dark-gleaming wave stood\nup around them, mountain-high,
arched over, and hid the god and the mortal woman.
He loosed the girdle of her maidenhood,\nand poured sleep over her.
And when the god had finished the works of love,\nhe clamped a hand on hers, and spoke a word, and named her:
'Rejoice in this love, woman. As the year turns round
you will bear glorious children — for the beds of the\nimmortals are not fruitless. Tend them, and rear them.
Now go home, and hold your peace, and name no name.
But know it: I am Poseidon, shaker of the earth.'
So speaking he plunged under the surging sea.
And she conceived, and bore Pelias and Neleus,\nwho both grew to be strong servants of great Zeus;
Pelias lived in wide-dancing-grounded Iolcus,\nrich in flocks, and Neleus in sandy Pylos.
And her other sons this queen\namong women bore to Cretheus:
Aeson, and Pheres, and Amythaon the chariot-fighter.
After her I saw Antiope, Asopus' daughter,\nwho could boast she had slept in the very arms of Zeus,
and she bore two sons, Amphion and Zethus,\nwho first founded the seat of seven-gated Thebes
and walled it round — for without walls they could not
live in wide-dancing-grounded Thebes,\nstrong though they were.
After her I saw Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife,\nwho bore Heracles, the lion-hearted, bold in the fight,
after she lay mingled in the arms of great Zeus;\nand Megara, daughter of high-spirited Creon,
whom Amphitryon's son held as wife —\nthe man whose strength never wore.
And I saw the mother of Oedipus, beautiful Epicaste,\nwho did a monstrous thing in the ignorance of her mind,
marrying her own son; and he, who had killed his father,
married her; and the gods made it known among men at once.
Yet he ruled on over the Cadmeians in lovely Thebes,\nsuffering pains, through the gods' deadly designs;
and she went down to the house of\nHades, strong warden of the gate,
fastening a noose to hang sheer from the high roof-beam,
gripped by her anguish — and left behind for him the pains
past counting that a mother's Furies bring to pass.
And I saw Chloris, beautiful\npast telling, whom Neleus once
married for her beauty, bringing bride-gifts past number:
youngest daughter of Amphion, Iasus' son,\nwho once ruled in strength in Minyan Orchomenus.
She was queen of Pylos, and bore him shining children:
Nestor, and Chromius, and lordly Periclymenus,\nand after them she bore that wonder of mortals, strong Pero,
whom all the neighboring men were courting;\nbut Neleus would give her to no man who could not drive off
the crook-horned, broad-browed cattle of mighty Iphicles
out of Phylace — a dangerous herd. Only the blameless seer
undertook to drive them; and the\nhard doom of a god bound him fast,
the cruel bonds, and the herdsmen of the wild.
But when at last the months and the\ndays were coming to fulfillment,
as the year rolled round and the seasons came again,\nthen at last mighty Iphicles set him free,
when he had told out all the decrees of fate.\nAnd the design of Zeus was accomplished.
And I saw Leda, wife of Tyndareus,\nwho bore to Tyndareus two strong-hearted sons:
Castor the horse-breaker,\nand Polydeuces good with his fists.
These two the life-giving earth\nholds — both of them living:
even under the earth they have honor from Zeus,\nand live turn about, one day each in turn,
and each in turn are dead.\nThey have won honor equal to the gods'.
After her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus,\nwho could say that she had lain with Poseidon,
and she bore two sons — but short-lived they proved —\ngodlike Otus, and far-famed Ephialtes:
the tallest men the grain-giving earth ever nourished,\nand far the most beautiful, after famous Orion.
At nine years old they measured nine\ncubits across, and stood nine fathoms high;
To carry the din of furious war up into Olympus.
Ossa they strained to pile on Olympus, and on Ossa\nPelion of the shivering leaves, to make heaven scalable.
And they would have accomplished it,\nhad they reached the measure of manhood;
but the son of Zeus,\nwhom fair-haired Leto bore, destroyed them
both, before the down had bloomed beneath their temples
and thickened on their chins\nin the flower of a young beard.
And Phaedra I saw, and Procris, and beautiful Ariadne,
the daughter of Minos the deadly-minded, whom Theseus once
carried off from Crete, making for the hill of holy
Athens — and had no joy of her: Artemis killed her first,\non sea-ringed Dia, on the testimony of Dionysus.
And Maera I saw, and Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle,\nwho took precious gold as the price of her own husband.
But all of them I could not tell through or name —\nall the wives and daughters of heroes I saw there:
the divine night would waste\naway first. No — it is the hour
for sleep, whether I go down to the fast ship and the crew
or stay here. My sending rests\nwith the gods, and with you."
So he spoke; and they were all hushed in silence,\nheld fast under the spell, through the shadowy halls.
And white-armed Arete began to speak among them:
"Phaeacians — how does this man appear to you now:
his looks, his stature, the balanced mind within?
And he is my guest — though each of you shares the honor.
Do not hurry, then, to send him off, and do not cut short
your gifts to one so needy: for many are the\ntreasures lying in your halls by the gods' good will."
And among them spoke the old hero Echeneus,\nthe man elder-born beyond the other Phaeacians:
"Friends — not wide of the mark,\nnot short of our own thought,
are the words of our watchful-minded queen. Heed them.
But on Alcinous here depend both word and deed."
Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and said:
"This word shall stand — so surely as I\nlive and rule the oar-loving Phaeacians.
Let the guest endure it, then,\nfor all his hunger for homecoming:
let him stay till tomorrow, until I make our whole\ngift complete. His sending shall be the men's concern —
all men's, and mine above all:\nfor mine is the power in this land.
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Lord Alcinous, most renowned among all peoples,\nif you bade me stay here even for a year
and readied my sending, and gave me shining gifts,\neven that I would choose; and it would profit me far more
to come to my own dear country with a fuller hand:
so should I be more honored, and more dear,\nto all the men who saw me sailing home to Ithaca."
Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and said:
"Odysseus — looking at you, we cannot liken you to\na cheat or a thief — the kind the black earth breeds
in such crops, scattered everywhere:
men who build lies out of what no eye could ever test.
There is a shape upon your words,\nand a noble mind within them,
and you have told your tale\nwith knowledge, like a singer —
the grim sorrows of all the Argives, and your own.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
did you see any of your godlike companions,\nwho went to Ilium with you, and met their doom there?
This night is long — marvelously long. It is not yet\ntime to sleep in the hall. Tell me the deeds of wonder.
I could hold out until the shining dawn, if only you\ncould bear, here in the hall, to tell me your sorrows."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Lord Alcinous, most renowned among all peoples —\nthere is an hour for many tales, and an hour for sleep.
But if you long to listen still, I would not grudge\nyou the telling of things more pitiful still:
the sorrows of my companions, who perished afterward —
Battle-cry and its groaning
only to die on the homeward way, by an evil woman's will.
Now when holy Persephone had scattered\nthe women's souls this way and that,
there came the soul of Agamemnon, Atreus' son,\ngrieving; and around him others were gathered — all who
died with him in the house of\nAegisthus, and met their doom.
He knew me at once, when he had drunk the dark blood,
and he wept, shrill and loud, letting the big tears fall,
stretching his hands toward me, straining to reach me —
but there was no strength grounded in him now,\nno force such as once filled his supple limbs.
I wept to see him, and my heart pitied him,\nand lifting my voice I spoke winged words to him:
'Most glorious son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men —\nwhat doom of death, that lays men low, mastered you?
Did Poseidon master you in your ships,\nrousing the wretched blast of hard winds?
Or did hostile men cut you down on dry land as you\ncarved away their cattle and their fine flocks of sheep,
or fought them for their city and their women?'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices:
Poseidon did not master me in my ships,\nrousing the wretched blast of hard winds,
and hostile men did not cut me down on dry land.
Aegisthus built my death and my doom, and killed me —\nwith my cursed wife — after calling me to his house
and feasting me: as a man cuts down an ox at the manger.
So I died the most pitiable of\ndeaths; and around me my other
companions were killed without pause, like white-tusked
swine slaughtered in the house of a rich and powerful man
for a wedding, a club-feast, or a swelling banquet.
You have stood in the killing of many men before now,\ncut down singly, or in the crush of battle —
but you would have grieved at\nheart above all to see that sight:
how around the wine-bowl and the loaded tables we lay\nin the hall, and the whole floor steamed with blood.
And the most pitiful voice I\nheard was Priam's daughter's —
Cassandra's, whom Clytemnestra\nof the crooked counsels killed
over my body; and I, dying, tried to raise my hands
and beat them down on the sword-blade —\nand she, the bitch-faced,
turned her back: she could not bring herself,\nthough I was going down to Hades,
to draw my eyelids shut with her hands, or close my mouth.
So true it is that nothing is more dread,\nmore dog-shameless, than a woman
who can set her mind on deeds like these —\nthe way that woman plotted her unspeakable work,
building the murder of her own\nwedded husband. And I had thought
to come home welcome to my children and my slaves!
But she — that mistress of atrocity — has poured out\nshame on her own head, and on all women after her,
the female kind — yes, even on the doer of good.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Ah, gods — how terribly has Zeus of the wide voice hated
the seed of Atreus from the beginning,\nand through the designs
of women: for Helen's sake we died in our thousands,
and for you Clytemnestra set her\nsnare while you were far away.'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'Then never be gentle, you too, even to your own wife.
Do not tell out to her the whole word that you know:
say part, and let part stay hidden.
But not for you, Odysseus, will murder come from a wife.
Too understanding she is,\ntoo watchful the mind in her breast —
the daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope.
A young bride we left her, when we went\nto the war; and a boy was at her breast,
an infant, who now, I suppose, sits numbered among men —
the fortunate one! His dear\nfather will see him, coming home,
and he will embrace his father:\nthat is the right way of things.
But my wife did not let me fill even my eyes
with my own son. She killed me\nbefore that — killed the man himself.
And I will tell you another thing:\nlay it up in your heart.
In secret — not in the open — bring your ship in
to your own dear country.\nFor there is no trusting women any more.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
do you hear whether my son is still alive,\nsomewhere — in Orchomenus perhaps, or in sandy Pylos,
or with Menelaus in wide Sparta?
For noble Orestes has not yet died on the earth.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Son of Atreus, why ask me this? I know nothing —
whether he lives or is dead.\nIt is evil to speak words empty as wind.'
So the two of us stood trading grim words,\ngrieving, letting the big tears fall.
And there came the soul of Achilles, Peleus' son,\nand of Patroclus, and of blameless Antilochus,
and of Ajax, who was first in beauty and in body of\nall the Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus.
And the soul of swift-footed Aeacides knew me,\nand mourning he spoke winged words to me:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —
reckless man! What deed will your\nmind plot now, still greater?
How did you dare come down to Hades, where the dead\nlive without wits — the phantoms of worn-out mortals?'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Achilles, son of Peleus,\nfar the mightiest of the Achaeans —
I came for Tiresias, out of need: in hope he\nmight tell some plan for reaching rugged Ithaca.
For not yet have I come near Achaea — not yet
set foot on my own land: evil is\nwith me always. But you, Achilles —
no man before you was more blessed,\nand none will be after:
living, we Argives honored you like the gods,\nand now you rule in strength among the dead,
here where you are.\nDo not grieve at dying, then, Achilles.'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'Do not talk death over sweetly to me, shining Odysseus.
I would rather be bound to the\nplow-land, hired out to another —
some man without a land-lot, without much living —\nthan be king over all the wasted dead.
Enough — tell me word of that proud son of mine:
did he follow to the war, to be a champion, or did he not?
And tell me of blameless Peleus, if you have heard:
does he still hold his honor among the Myrmidon crowds,\nor do they slight him now through Hellas and Phthia,
because old age has hold of him, hand and foot?
For I am no longer his defender under the rays of\nthe sun — no longer the man I was when in wide Troy
I cut down the best of their host,\nin the Argives' defense.
Could I come, that man,\neven for an hour, to my father's house,
I would make my fury and my unconquerable hands a horror
to those who do him violence and shut him from his honor.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Of blameless Peleus I have heard nothing.
But of your own dear son, Neoptolemus,\nI will tell you the whole truth, as you ask.
I myself carried him, in my trim hollow ship,\nout of Scyros to join the strong-greaved Achaeans.
And whenever we framed our\ncounsels around the city of Troy,
he was always first to speak, and his words never missed:
godlike Nestor and I alone outdid him.
And whenever we fought on the\nTrojan plain with the bronze,
he never lingered back in the mass of men or the crush,
but ran far out in front, yielding his fury to no one,\nand he cut down many men in the terrible fighting.
All of them I could not tell through or name —\nall the host he killed in the Argives' defense;
but such a man was the son of Telephus\nhe brought down with the bronze,
the hero Eurypylus — and around him his Ceteian
companions in crowds were slain,\nfor the sake of a woman's gifts.
He was the handsomest man I ever saw, after noble Memnon.
And when we climbed down into the horse Epeius built —\nwe, the best of the Argives — and it all lay upon me,
to throw open our close-packed ambush or to shut it,\nthen the other leaders and counselors of the Danaans
kept wiping tears away, and each man's legs shook\nunder him; but him — never once did my eyes see
his beautiful skin go pale, or catch him wiping a\ntear from his cheeks. No: he begged me, over and over,
to let him out of the horse,\nand kept fingering his sword-hilt
and his spear heavy with bronze,\nwith evil in his heart for the Trojans.
And when we had sacked the steep city of Priam,
he boarded his ship with his\nshare and a fine prize of honor —
never touched by a thrown spear, never gashed\nin the close work, the way it happens so often
in war. For Ares rages blind, and makes no distinctions.'
So I spoke; and the soul of swift-footed Aeacides went\naway with long strides across the meadow of asphodel,
rejoicing that I had said his son was preeminent.
And the other souls of the dead who are gone stood\ngrieving, and each asked after what was dear to it.
Alone of them all, the soul of Ajax, Telamon's son,\nstood apart, still raging over the victory
I won against him, pleading my case by the ships,
for the arms of Achilles.\nHis honored mother set the prize,
and the sons of the Trojans judged it, and Pallas Athena.
Would to god I had never won a contest like that one:
such a head the earth closed over for those arms' sake —
Ajax, who in beauty and in every deed of war stood first
of all the Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus.
Him I addressed with honeyed words:
'Ajax, son of blameless Telamon — could you not, then,
even in death forget your anger at me for those cursed arms?\nThe gods made them a scourge for the Argives —
such a tower fell when you fell. For you the\nAchaeans grieve without ceasing, as for the very head
of Achilles, Peleus' son. And no one else bears the\nblame, but Zeus: he hated the army of the Danaan
spearmen with a terrible hatred,\nand laid your doom on you.
Come here, lord — come hear our word, our speech.
Master your fury; break that proud heart down.'
So I spoke. He answered me nothing. He went his way
after the other souls, into the\nErebus of the dead who are gone.
There, even so, for all his anger, he might yet have\nspoken to me, or I to him. But the heart in my breast
wished to see the souls of the other dead.
There I saw Minos, the shining son of Zeus,\nholding a golden scepter, delivering law among the dead —
he seated, and around him the dead\npleading their cases before the lord,
sitting and standing through\nthe wide-gated house of Hades.
And after him I marked out huge Orion herding the\nwild beasts together across the meadow of asphodel —
the very beasts he had killed on the lonely mountains —\na club in his hands, all bronze, forever unbroken.
And I saw Tityus, the son of glorious Earth,\nlaid out on the ground: over nine roods he sprawled,
and two vultures, sitting either side, tore at his liver,
plunging into the caul;\nand his hands could not beat them off:
for he had assaulted Leto, the honored consort of Zeus,
as she walked toward Pytho through\nPanopeus of the lovely dancing-grounds.
And Tantalus too I saw, holding his hard agonies,\nstanding in a pool that lapped against his chin —
and he strained with thirst,\nand could not reach a drop to drink:
as often as the old man stooped, in a fury to drink,
so often the water was swallowed\naway and gone, and around his feet
the black earth showed, parched dry by a god.
And trees in tall leaf poured their fruit above his head,
pears and pomegranates and apple trees bright with\nfruit, sweet figs and olives in full flourish;
and whenever the old man reached\nout to close his hands on them,
the wind would toss them away toward the shadowing clouds.
And Sisyphus too I saw, holding his hard agonies,\nwrestling a monstrous stone with both his arms.
Bracing himself — straining with hands and feet —
he would shove the stone uphill\ntoward the crest; but each time,
just as he was about to heave it over the top,\nthe sheer weight wheeled it round,
and down to the plain again rolled the shameless stone.
And he would strain again, and shove — the sweat\nstreaming off his limbs, and the dust rising off his head.
And after him I marked the strength of Heracles —
his phantom: for the man himself,\namong the deathless gods,
delights in the feasting,\nwith fair-ankled Hebe for his wife,
the child of great Zeus and of Hera of the golden sandals.
Around that phantom rose a clamor of the dead, like birds
scattering in panic every way. And he, like black night,\nthe bow bare in his hand, an arrow on the string,
glared terribly about him, forever\nlike a man on the point of shooting.
And terrible was the baldric crossing his chest,
the sword-belt all of gold,\nwhere deeds of wonder had been worked —
bears, and wild boars, and lions with fire in their eyes,
and combats, and battles,\nand murders, and the killings of men.
May the man who designed that belt design nothing\nfurther — whoever took such work into his craft!
And he in his turn knew me, the moment his eyes fell\non me, and mourning he spoke winged words to me:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —\npoor man! So you too are dragging out an evil doom
such as I bore beneath the rays of the sun?
I was a son of Zeus, of Cronos' line — and my misery\nhad no end: for I was bound in service to a man
far worse than I, who laid hard labors on me,\nand once he sent me here, to fetch the Hound: no other
labor, he reckoned, could be mightier than that one.
I carried the Hound up and out of Hades,\nand Hermes saw me on my way, and gray-eyed Athena.'
So speaking he went back into the house of Hades;
but I stayed rooted there, in hope some other might\nyet come of the hero men who died in the time before.
And now I would have seen still\nearlier men, the ones I longed for —
Theseus and Pirithous, glorious children of the gods —
but first the tribes of the dead came gathering, thousand
on thousand, with a sound that had no\nearthly likeness; and the pale terror took me
that queenly Persephone might send out of Hades\nthe Gorgon head of the dread monster against me.
Straight to the ship I went, and ordered my companions\nto board in their turn and loose the stern-cables;
and they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks.
And the wave of the current bore\nher down the river of Ocean —
the rowing first; and afterward,\na beautiful following wind.
